Read the transcript of the audio guide
  1. In July 1935 an American vice consul in Shanghai pinned a small photograph to a form, and an eighteen-year-old student signed his name across it: Ieoh-ming Pe. source
  2. His father, Tsuyee Pei, was a manager at the Bank of China. source
  3. He sailed on the steamship President Coolidge and arrived at San Francisco on 28 August 1935. source
  4. He was admitted as a student under the Immigration Act of 1924, which allowed in Chinese students at a time when almost all other Chinese immigration to the United States was banned. source
  5. Because the consulate in Shanghai had spelled his name "Pe," that is the name on his early American papers. source
  6. Pei started at the University of Pennsylvania but soon moved to the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. source
  7. Then, in 1937, war broke out between China and Japan, followed by the Second World War. source
  8. Going home became more and more difficult. source
  9. By 1946 he was married to Eileen Loo and teaching at Harvard. source
  10. Harvard asked for him to stay one more year as a teaching fellow. source
  11. The immigration officers agreed, but noted: source
  12. It is understood that the subject expects to return to China to teach after this year's work at Harvard. source
  13. To change from a visiting student to a permanent resident, Pei and his wife had to leave the United States and apply from outside. source
  14. They went to Canada, received immigrant visas at Saint John, New Brunswick, on 23 September 1947, and crossed back into the United States at Calais, Maine, three days later. source
  15. Twelve years after he arrived, he was finally allowed to stay. source
  16. His most famous design is the glass pyramid that forms the main entrance of the Louvre in Paris. source
  17. What would make you stay in a country that kept telling you your visit was only temporary?
Read the transcript of the short and the video
  1. In July 1935 an American vice consul in Shanghai pinned a small photograph to a form, and an eighteen-year-old student signed his name across it: Ieoh-ming Pe. source
  2. I. M. Pei came to America on a two-year student visa. source
  3. For twelve years the government expected him to go home. source
  4. He stayed, became one of the most celebrated architects in the world, and put a glass pyramid in front of the Louvre. source
  5. His immigration file, all 139 pages of it, survives at the National Archives. source
  6. To change from a visiting student to a permanent resident, Pei and his wife had to leave the United States and apply from outside. source
  7. Twelve years after he arrived, he was finally allowed to stay. source
  8. Read the full story, with every source, on this page.
